cse-2004-cs-1.approach: Recall what structured programming is for: building programs only from single-entry/single-exit sequence, selection and iteration blocks so the run-time flow of control can be read straight off the source text.

steps.title: The building blocks
steps.body: A structured program is composed only of **sequence**, **selection** (`if/else`, `switch`) and **iteration** (`while`, `for`) blocks, each with exactly one entry and one exit, nested properly. Böhm–Jacopini showed these three suffice for any computable flow.

steps.title: What this buys
steps.body: Because blocks nest, the textual order of the source mirrors the dynamic execution order. A reader (or a proof of correctness) can follow the **flow of control from the program text** without chasing jumps.

steps.title: Goal versus means
steps.body: Avoiding `goto` is the usual *means* (Dijkstra, "Go To Statement Considered Harmful"), and indentation merely displays the structure. The *goal* is readability of control flow in the source — option C.

answer.value: be able to infer the flow of control from the program text

optionAnalysis.reason: Indentation is cosmetic; a goto-ridden program can still be neatly indented.
Compiled code is machine code full of jumps; structured programming is about the source, not the object code.
This is the purpose: the static text reveals the dynamic flow of control.
Avoiding GOTO is a technique used to reach the goal, not the goal itself (and a disciplined goto can still be structured).

pitfalls: Choosing "avoid GOTO" — it is the best-known slogan but it is the means, not the end.
cse-2004-cs-1.verification: Matches Dijkstra's argument: the point of removing goto is to make the process (execution) correspond to the program text.

cse-2004-cs-2.approach: C passes arguments by value: swap receives copies of x and y, so exchanging the copies leaves the caller's variables untouched.

steps.title: Trace swap(x, y)
steps.body: Say $x=1,\ y=2$. On the call, new locals $a=1,\ b=2$ are created. Inside: $\text{temp}=1$, $a=2$, $b=1$. On return $a, b$ are destroyed; $x=1,\ y=2$ — unchanged.

steps.title: Why swap(&x, &y) is no fix
steps.body: The parameters are declared `int`, not `int *`. Passing `&x` would pass an address that is then treated as a plain integer copy; the function still only swaps its local copies (and it is a type mismatch).

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The function as written cannot exchange the caller's values because the **parameters are passed by value**. A working version needs `void swap(int *a, int *b)` with `*a`, `*b` inside.

answer.value: swap(x, y) cannot be used as the parameters are passed by value

With int parameters the addresses are just copied into a and b and swapped locally; the function never dereferences them.
A function need not return a value to have an effect (it could modify through pointers); void is not the problem.
Correct: call by value means the changes never reach x and y.

pitfalls: Thinking `&x` alone makes it call-by-reference — the callee must also dereference pointers.

steps.title: Why this is "efficient"
steps.body: Neither stack has a fixed half: one stack may use 90% of the array if the other is small. Only the adjacency test lets every cell be used.

cse-2004-cs-5.approach: Parentheses must close in the reverse order they open (last opened, first closed) — exactly LIFO, so a stack is the natural structure.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Scan left to right. On `(` **push**; on `)` **pop** — if the stack is empty, the expression is unbalanced. At the end the stack must be empty.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: `((a+b)*c)`: push, push, pop (after b), pop (after c) → stack empty → balanced. `(a+b))`: the second `)` finds an empty stack → unbalanced.

steps.title: Why a stack
steps.body: With mixed brackets `([)]`, each closer must match the **most recent** unmatched opener — a LIFO property a queue (FIFO) cannot give.

cse-2004-cs-6.approach: Level order visits all nodes at depth 0, then depth 1, then depth 2, … — exactly the order in which breadth-first search (with a queue) discovers them.

steps.title: BFS from the root
steps.body: Enqueue the root. Repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it, and enqueue its children left to right. All depth-$d$ nodes are dequeued before any depth-$(d+1)$ node.

steps.title: Link-time
steps.body: The linker combines the object files of $M_1$ and $M_2$, finds the definition exported by $M_2$, and patches the reference. Hence **link-time**. (Load-time fixes only relocation of addresses; dynamic linking is not implied here.)

cse-2004-cs-10.approach: With one register and the left operand required in it, evaluate E2 first and park it in memory; then E1 ends in the register and SUB can use E2 straight from memory — no extra store/reload of E1.

steps.title: E1 first
steps.body: Compute E1 into R. Now E2 needs R, so E1 must be **stored** to temp T1; compute E2 in R; but SUB needs E1 in R, so store E2 to T2, **load** T1 back, then `SUB R, T2`. Two extra stores and one extra load.

steps.title: E2 first
steps.body: Compute E2 into R, store to T. Compute E1 into R (it is already where SUB needs it), then `SUB R, T`. Only one spill.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Evaluating $E_2$ first gives strictly shorter code, so the order matters and E2 should go first.

optionAnalysis.reason: E1 first forces E1 to be saved and later reloaded into the register — longer code.
